questions.q: What does setting `transactional.id` on a producer do?

options.t: It enables transactions and idempotence, and fences older instances
It makes every send() block until the record is committed
options.why: Sends are still asynchronous; commits happen through commitTransaction().

options.t: It is only a label for logging, like client.id
options.why: It enables transactions and identifies the producer across restarts.

options.t: It makes the producer write all records to a hidden transactional topic first
options.why: Records go to their normal topics; markers decide visibility.

questions.explain: `transactional.id` enables transactions and implies idempotence. Reusing it after a crash lets the new instance abort the old instance's open transaction, fencing it.

questions.q: A transactional producer calls `beginTransaction()` while a transaction is already open. Why is that a mistake?

options.t: Transactions must each use a different topic
options.why: A transaction can span several topics and partitions.

options.t: A producer can have only one open transaction at a time
beginTransaction() can only be called once in a producer's life
options.why: A producer runs many transactions, one after another.

options.t: The broker allows one transaction per partition at a time
options.why: The limit is per producer: one open transaction.

questions.explain: The Javadoc notes there can be only one open transaction per producer; the next one starts after the current one is committed or aborted.

questions.q: Inside a transaction, `commitTransaction()` throws `ProducerFencedException`. What should the application do?

options.t: Call abortTransaction() and retry the same transaction
options.why: Fencing is fatal; abort can't recover a fenced producer.

options.t: Retry commitTransaction() until it succeeds
options.why: A fenced producer stays fenced.

options.t: Close the producer: another instance has taken over
Lower transaction.timeout.ms and continue
options.why: Timeouts don't undo fencing.

questions.explain: `ProducerFencedException`, `OutOfOrderSequenceException`, `UnsupportedVersionException` and `AuthorizationException` are fatal for a transactional producer: the only option is `close()`. Other errors: abort the transaction and try again.

questions.q: A consume-transform-produce application aborts a transaction after processing records from offsets 100-149. What must it do next to avoid skipping those records?

options.t: Nothing; the consumer rewinds itself when the transaction aborts
options.why: The stored position reverts, but the consumer doesn't rewind its in-memory position.

options.t: Commit offset 150 with commitSync()
options.why: That would skip the records whose output was aborted.

options.t: Restart the brokers
options.why: Nothing on the brokers needs restarting.

options.t: Seek back to the last committed offsets

questions.explain: After an abort the committed offsets revert, but the consumer must refetch them itself: the application resets its position (or recreates producer and consumer, which rewinds to the last committed offset).

questions.q: In a transactional consume-transform-produce loop, which TWO consumer settings are needed?

options.t: enable.auto.commit=false
auto.offset.reset=none
options.why: That only decides what happens with no committed offset.

options.t: isolation.level=read_committed
max.poll.records=1
options.why: Batch size doesn't matter to transactions.

options.t: group.protocol=classic
options.why: Either group protocol works.

questions.explain: For transactions the consumer turns auto-commit off (offsets go through the producer's transaction) and reads with `read_committed`.

questions.q: A transaction stays open for 2 minutes with `transaction.timeout.ms` at its default. What happens?

options.t: The transaction coordinator aborts it, because it was open longer than 60 s
Nothing; transactions have no time limit
options.why: transaction.timeout.ms (default 1 minute) limits them.

options.t: The producer commits it automatically
options.why: A timed-out transaction is aborted, never committed.

options.t: The broker raises it to 15 minutes
options.why: 15 minutes is the broker's cap on what clients may request.

questions.explain: The coordinator aborts a transaction open longer than `transaction.timeout.ms` (default 60 000 ms). The broker's `transaction.max.timeout.ms` (15 min) caps what a client may set.

questions.q: A tool must read exactly partitions 0 and 3 of a topic, with no consumer group rebalancing. Which API fits?

options.t: subscribe() with a regular expression
options.why: subscribe uses group management, so the group decides the partitions.

options.t: assign() with the two TopicPartitions
subscribe() and then assign() for the two partitions
options.why: Subscription and manual assignment can't be combined.

options.t: seekToEnd() with no subscription
options.why: A consumer must subscribe or assign before polling or seeking.

questions.explain: `assign()` is manual assignment: it doesn't use group management, so no rebalance happens. It cannot be combined with `subscribe()`.

questions.q: A consumer is subscribed to `orders`. The code later calls `subscribe(List.of("payments"))`. What is it subscribed to now?

options.t: orders and payments
options.why: Subscriptions are not incremental.

options.t: Nothing; the second call fails
options.why: A new subscribe call is allowed and replaces the old one.

options.t: orders until the next rebalance, then both
options.why: The new list replaces the old one.

options.t: Only payments: a new subscription replaces the old one

questions.explain: Topic subscriptions are not incremental: the new list replaces the current one.

questions.q: What does `consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))` return when records are already available?

options.t: It returns them at once, without waiting the full 500 ms
It always waits 500 ms, then returns everything that arrived
options.why: It returns immediately if records are available.

options.t: It returns one record per call
options.why: It returns a batch, up to max.poll.records.

options.t: It throws if fewer than fetch.min.bytes are available
options.why: fetch.min.bytes affects the broker's wait, not an exception.

questions.explain: `poll` returns immediately if records are available; otherwise it waits up to the timeout and returns an empty set if none arrive.

questions.q: After a bug fix, a consumer must reprocess partition 2 of `orders` from offset 5000. Which call does that?

options.t: commitSync() with offset 5000, then wait for a rebalance
options.why: That changes the stored offset, but not the running consumer's position.

options.t: seekToBeginning() on all partitions
options.why: That rewinds everything to the start, not to 5000.

options.t: seek(new TopicPartition("orders", 2), 5000)
pause() then resume() on partition 2
options.why: Pausing doesn't change position.

questions.explain: `seek(partition, offset)` overrides the offset the next `poll` fetches from; consumers can rewind to re-consume after a bug fix.

questions.q: What is the difference between `commitSync()` and `commitAsync()`?

options.t: commitSync commits on the broker; commitAsync commits on the client
options.why: Both store offsets in Kafka.

options.t: commitAsync commits only every 5 seconds
options.why: That is auto-commit's interval.

options.t: commitSync blocks until done; commitAsync returns at once
commitAsync commits to a different internal topic
options.why: Both write to the same offsets store.

questions.explain: `commitSync` blocks until the commit succeeds or fails; `commitAsync` doesn't block.

questions.q: A consumer commits manually after processing. Where should it commit what it has processed so that a rebalance doesn't cause another member to repeat that work?

options.t: In onPartitionsRevoked, before the partitions move
In onPartitionsAssigned of the consumer that receives the partitions
options.why: By then the partitions have moved; the new owner can't commit the old owner's progress.

options.t: In a shutdown hook only
options.why: Rebalances happen while the application is running.

options.t: Nowhere; Kafka commits on rebalance automatically for manual-commit consumers
options.why: With auto-commit off, nothing is committed for you.

questions.explain: `onPartitionsRevoked` runs before revoked partitions go to another consumer: the place to commit what was processed.

questions.q: An application shares one KafkaConsumer between two threads, one polling and one committing. What is wrong with this?

options.t: Nothing; KafkaConsumer is thread safe
options.why: The consumer is not thread safe.

options.t: Committing needs its own group.id
options.why: Commits belong to the consumer's own group.

options.t: Only one thread may open a TCP connection to the brokers at a time
options.why: The issue is thread safety of the consumer object.

options.t: The consumer isn't thread safe; only wakeup() may cross threads

questions.explain: The consumer is not thread safe. The one exception is `wakeup()`, which another thread can call to break a blocking `poll` with `WakeupException`.

questions.q: A consumer's downstream database is overloaded, so it calls `pause()` on its partitions. What must it keep doing to keep them?

options.t: Nothing; paused partitions are held for an hour
options.why: Membership still depends on calling poll.

options.t: Keep calling poll()
Commit every second
options.why: Commits don't keep a member in the group.

options.t: Call wakeup() in a loop
options.why: wakeup() only interrupts a blocking poll.

questions.explain: `pause()` stops records from paused partitions in later polls, but "as long as you continue to call poll, the consumer will stay in the group".

questions.q: A consumer sets `fetch.min.bytes=100000` and `fetch.max.wait.ms=500`. A partition has only 2 KB of new data. What does the broker do?

options.t: Waits until 100 KB have arrived, however long that takes
options.why: fetch.max.wait.ms caps the wait.

options.t: Returns an error because there isn't enough data
options.why: It returns what it has after the wait.

options.t: Waits up to 500 ms for more data, then returns what it has
Returns the 2 KB at once
options.why: It first waits up to fetch.max.wait.ms for fetch.min.bytes.

questions.explain: The broker waits for `fetch.min.bytes` of data or `fetch.max.wait.ms`, whichever comes first. Larger values raise throughput a little and add latency.

questions.q: A consumer takes about 2 seconds per record. With `max.poll.records` at its default, why is it being removed from its group?

options.t: A poll returns up to 500 records: over 16 minutes of work
fetch.max.bytes is too small
options.why: Fetch size doesn't cause removal from the group.

options.t: The session timeout is shorter than the heartbeat interval
options.why: These are defaults that work; the issue is time between polls.

options.t: max.poll.records limits how much the broker sends
options.why: It limits records per poll, not fetching.

questions.explain: `max.poll.records` defaults to 500; at 2 s each a batch takes over 16 minutes, far beyond `max.poll.interval.ms` (5 minutes). Lowering it, or processing faster, keeps polls frequent.

questions.q: A single record batch in a partition is 3 MiB, larger than `max.partition.fetch.bytes` (1 MiB). Does the consumer get stuck?

options.t: Yes; it must raise the setting before it can progress
options.why: The limit is not absolute.

options.t: Yes; the broker deletes the batch
options.why: Brokers don't delete data for a consumer's limit.

options.t: No; the broker splits the batch into 1 MiB pieces
options.why: Batches are not split.

options.t: No; an oversized first batch is still returned

questions.explain: `max.partition.fetch.bytes` and `fetch.max.bytes` are not absolute: a first batch larger than the limit is still returned so the consumer can make progress.

questions.q: A consumer writes results to a relational database and wants exactly-once results without Kafka transactions. Which approach does the KafkaConsumer Javadoc describe?

options.t: Use auto-commit with a short interval, so very few records are ever at risk
options.why: Auto-commit can't be atomic with the database write.

options.t: Store each offset with its result in the database; seek on restart
Use acks=all on the consumer
options.why: acks is a producer setting.

options.t: Commit before writing to the database
options.why: That gives at-most-once.

questions.explain: Storing offsets outside Kafka: turn off auto-commit, store each offset with the output atomically, and on restart `seek` to the stored offset (with a rebalance listener when partitions are assigned by the group).

questions.q: A plain Java consumer hits a record its deserializer can't read. What happens, and what can the application do?

options.t: poll() throws RecordDeserializationException; the app decides what to do
The client sends it to a built-in dead-letter topic automatically and carries on
options.why: The Apache Kafka client has no built-in dead-letter topic.

options.t: The record is skipped silently and the consumer continues
options.why: The consumer won't move past it by itself.

options.t: The broker deletes the bad record
options.why: Brokers don't inspect or delete records for consumers.

questions.explain: `poll` throws `RecordDeserializationException`, carrying the topic-partition and offset. The consumer doesn't move past it by itself; the application decides what to do, such as a dead-letter topic and a `seek` past it.

questions.q: Which TWO statements about consumer commit failures are right?

options.t: CommitFailedException can follow when the consumer was removed from the group for exceeding max.poll.interval.ms
RetriableCommitFailedException is a retriable exception
Committed offsets are stored in the topic being consumed
options.why: Committed offsets go to the internal offsets topic, __consumer_offsets.

options.t: A commit failure deletes the records from the topic
options.why: Commits never change the log.

options.t: Commits fail whenever auto.offset.reset=latest
options.why: auto.offset.reset doesn't affect commits.

questions.explain: A consumer that left the group for not polling gets `CommitFailedException` on a later `commitSync`. `RetriableCommitFailedException` is a subclass of `RetriableException`.

questions.q: What is `group.id` needed for on a consumer?

options.t: To connect to the cluster at all
options.why: bootstrap.servers is what's needed to connect.

options.t: To choose the compression codec
options.why: Compression is chosen by producers.

options.t: To use subscribe() with group management, or Kafka-based offset storage
To read from a single partition with assign()
options.why: Manual assignment can work without group management.

questions.explain: `group.id` is required to use group management (`subscribe`) or Kafka-based offset storage.
